learningObjectives.title: Migration: impacts on source and host areas

questions.q: Which statement best defines globalisation?
options: The process by which the world's economies, societies and cultures become increasingly interconnected
The movement of people permanently from one country to another
A company that operates factories in more than one country
The growth of a single country's manufacturing industry
questions.explain: Globalisation describes the increasing interconnection and interdependence of the world's economies, societies and cultures.

questions.q: Which development has done most to speed up global communication and information flow?
options: The internet and satellite technology
The building of canals
The invention of the steam train
The spread of coal mining
questions.explain: The internet and satellite technology allow near-instant global communication, a key driver of globalisation.

questions.q: Why has globalisation increased rapidly in recent decades?
options: Improved transport, ICT and reduced trade barriers have connected countries more easily
Countries have become more isolated and self-sufficient
International trade has been banned in most regions
Air and sea transport have become much slower and costlier
questions.explain: Cheaper, faster transport, better communications technology and freer trade have all accelerated globalisation.

questions.q: What is containerisation?
options: The use of standard-sized steel containers to transport goods quickly and cheaply
The recycling of waste materials in shipping ports
The storage of grain in large silos
The packaging of food for local markets
questions.explain: Standardised shipping containers cut the cost and time of moving goods worldwide, boosting global trade.

questions.q: What is a transnational corporation (TNC)?
options: A company that operates in more than one country
A charity that works only within its home country
A government department that controls trade
A small business that trades locally
questions.explain: A TNC is a company with operations, such as offices or factories, in more than one country.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a transnational corporation?
options: Apple
A single village corner shop
A local family-run farm
A town's independent bakery
questions.explain: Apple designs, manufactures and sells products across many countries, making it a TNC.

questions.q: Why do many TNCs keep their headquarters in higher-income countries but locate manufacturing in lower-income countries?
options: To access skilled management at home while cutting production costs abroad
Because lower-income countries have the most expensive labour
To avoid selling any products in higher-income countries
Because manufacturing is illegal in higher-income countries
questions.explain: TNCs base HQ and research in HICs but shift production to countries with cheaper labour to reduce costs.

questions.q: Which is a benefit a TNC can bring to a lower-income host country?
options: Creation of jobs and inward investment
Guaranteed removal of all pollution
A fall in the country's total exports
An automatic end to poverty everywhere
questions.explain: TNCs can create employment, bring investment and transfer technology and skills to the host country.

questions.q: Which is a common disadvantage of TNCs for host countries?
options: Much of the profit is sent back to the company's home country
They always pay the highest wages in the country
They never employ any local workers
They refuse to sell goods anywhere in the world
questions.explain: Profits are often repatriated to the TNC's home country rather than staying in the host economy.

questions.q: A clothing TNC closes a factory in a lower-income country and moves it to a nearby country offering lower wages. This decision is mainly driven by the TNC's wish to:
options: Reduce production costs and increase profits
Increase the wages of its former workers
Reduce the number of countries it operates in
Stop selling clothes altogether
questions.explain: TNCs relocate production to wherever costs, especially labour, are lowest in order to maximise profit.

questions.q: What is migration?
options: The movement of people from one place to another to live
The trade of goods between two countries
The building of factories in another country
The growth of cities over time
questions.explain: Migration is the movement of people from one place to another, usually to live there.

questions.q: A farmer leaves a rural area after a severe drought destroys crops and there is no work. What best describes the drought and lack of work?
options: Push factors
Pull factors
Remittances
Economies of scale
questions.explain: Negative conditions such as drought and unemployment that drive people away from an area are push factors.

questions.q: Which pairing correctly matches a push factor with a pull factor?
options: Push: unemployment; Pull: better job opportunities
Push: safety and security; Pull: war and conflict
Push: higher wages; Pull: natural disaster
Push: good healthcare; Pull: famine
questions.explain: Push factors drive people from an area (e.g. unemployment); pull factors attract them to another (e.g. jobs).

questions.q: A country records 50,000 immigrants and 20,000 emigrants in one year. What is its net migration?
questions.explain: Net migration equals immigration minus emigration: 50,000 - 20,000 = +30,000.

questions.q: Which best describes a refugee?
options: A person forced to flee their country because of war, persecution or disaster
A person who moves country purely to earn higher wages
A person who moves within their own country for a new job
A tourist visiting another country for a short holiday
questions.explain: A refugee is forced to leave their country because of war, persecution or a natural disaster.

questions.q: What is an economic migrant?
options: A person who moves to another area or country to find work or a better standard of living
A person forced to flee because of persecution
A person who never leaves their home town
A person moving only for a family holiday
questions.explain: An economic migrant moves voluntarily, mainly to improve their job prospects and standard of living.

questions.q: What is meant by the 'brain drain' as an impact on a source country?
options: The loss of skilled and educated workers who emigrate
An increase in the number of schools built
The arrival of new industries and factories
A rise in the birth rate of the country
questions.explain: Brain drain is the loss of skilled, educated people from a source country when they emigrate for work.

questions.q: How do remittances benefit a migrant's source country?
options: Money sent home by migrants boosts family incomes and the local economy
They increase the number of skilled workers leaving
They reduce the country's total population instantly
They force the host country to pay higher taxes
questions.explain: Remittances are money sent home by migrants, raising family incomes and supporting the source economy.

questions.q: Which is a likely impact of immigration on a host country?
options: A larger workforce that can fill labour shortages
A guaranteed fall in the total population
The complete removal of all cultural diversity
An automatic end to all unemployment
questions.explain: Immigrants often add to the workforce, filling labour and skills shortages in the host country.

questions.q: Many people migrate from Mexico to the USA seeking higher-paid jobs and better services. This movement is best classified as:
options: International economic migration
Internal forced migration
Refugee movement caused by war
Seasonal migration within one country
questions.explain: Crossing an international border mainly for work and a better standard of living is international economic migration.

specSource: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Geography (4GE1) specification; Globalisation & Migration
